name: Besisahar
tagline: Lamjung's district town and the start of the Annapurna Circuit
meta_description: Besisahar (760 m), start of the Annapurna Circuit: buses from Kathmandu and Pokhara, jeeps to Chame and Manang, ACAP checkpost, hotels and tips.
summary: Besisahar is the headquarters of Lamjung district at 760 m in the Marsyangdi valley and the traditional starting point of the Annapurna Circuit. It is 6–7 hours by road from Kathmandu and 4 hours from Pokhara, with jeeps onward to Chame and Manang.
intro: Besisahar is a working market town rather than a mountain village. It stretches along a ridge above the Marsyangdi river, with government offices, banks, hardware shops and bus counters lining the main road. For decades trekkers began the Annapurna Circuit by walking out of the northern end of town, and although the road now continues all the way to Manang, Besisahar is still where most people switch from a bus to a four-wheel-drive jeep and where the ACAP permit is first checked.

The town sits in subtropical country, with rice terraces, banana trees and sal forest on the hillsides around it. On clear mornings in autumn and winter you can glimpse the snow of Lamjung Himal and Manaslu's southern ridges from the higher streets. The people of Lamjung are a mix of Gurung, Brahmin, Chhetri and Dalit communities, and the Gurung hill villages above the valley, such as Ghale Gaun and Bhujung, are known for homestay tourism.

Most trekkers spend only one night in Besisahar, or pass straight through. That is a pity only if you are interested in ordinary Nepali town life, which is easy to see here: tea shops serving sel roti at dawn, school children in uniform, buses being loaded with sacks of rice for upper villages. Practically, it is the last place on the circuit with reliable ATMs and full shops until Chame or Manang, so stock up on cash, snacks and any forgotten gear.
facts: Annapurna Circuit start, jeeps to Chame and Manang, Marsyangdi valley

highlights.title: Gateway to the Annapurna Circuit
highlights.text: Besisahar has been the official start of the Annapurna Circuit since the region opened to foreign trekkers in 1977. From here the route follows the Marsyangdi north and west for about 95 km to Manang before climbing to Thorong La at 5,416 m. The ACAP checkpost on the edge of town records every trekker heading up.

highlights.title: Jeep stand for the upper valley
highlights.text: Shared and private jeeps leave Besisahar each morning for Chame, about 6–7 hours, and Manang, about 9–10 hours. Seats can be booked at the counters near the bus park the evening before. This is the moment you decide how much of the lower circuit to drive and how much to walk.

highlights.title: Last full services before the mountains
highlights.text: Banks, several ATMs, pharmacies, mobile phone shops and general stores line the main road. Above Besisahar, cash machines are rare and unreliable until Chame, and prices rise with every day of portering. Buy snacks, a local SIM card, spare batteries and any medicine here rather than higher up.

highlights.title: Rice terraces of the lower Marsyangdi
highlights.text: The first stretch of the valley north of town, towards Bhulbhule and Bahundanda, is green and low, with rice terraces, bamboo and waterfalls. In October the terraces turn gold before harvest. Walkers who start here see the full change from subtropical farmland to high desert within a week.

highlights.title: Side trips to Gurung hill villages
highlights.text: Lamjung's hill villages above Besisahar, including Ghale Gaun and Bhujung, run community homestays with Gurung cultural programmes and views towards Lamjung Himal and the Annapurnas. They make a one- or two-night add-on before or after the circuit, reached by jeep in about 2–3 hours on rough roads.

how_to_reach.text: Kathmandu to Besisahar is about 175 km and 6–7 hours via the Prithvi Highway and Dumre. Pokhara to Besisahar is about 110 km and 4 hours. Tourist buses, local buses and private cars run daily; the Dumre to Besisahar section has improved but still slows near landslide zones.

Besisahar has no airport. The nearest is Pokhara, about 4 hours away by road. On the far side of the circuit, Jomsom airport links to Pokhara in about 20 minutes, which is why most itineraries start in Besisahar and finish with a flight out of Jomsom.

Walkers heading up the valley leave the north end of town and can follow the New Annapurna Trekking Trail sections on the opposite bank from the road, via Bhulbhule at 840 m and Bahundanda at 1,310 m, reaching Chame in about 5 days.

where_to_stay: Besisahar has a handful of mid-range hotels along the main road and near the bus park, plus simpler guesthouses aimed at trekkers and travelling Nepali businesspeople. Rooms usually come with attached bathrooms, hot water from solar or gas heaters, and Wi-Fi of variable speed. None are luxury properties, so think of it as a clean, practical overnight before the jeep ride. Book a room on the quieter side away from the bus park if you can, because buses start loading before dawn. On our circuit itineraries we reserve a standard hotel here for one night.
tips: Withdraw enough Nepali rupees in Besisahar for at least the first week of the circuit, as ATMs higher up are few and often empty.
Book jeep seats to Chame or Manang the evening before, and ask for a front or middle-row seat on the river side for the best views.
Carry your ACAP permit and passport copy in an easy pocket, as the checkpost on the edge of town will want to see them.
If you are prone to motion sickness, take medication before the jeep ride, which climbs on a rough, winding road for hours.
In the monsoon, check road conditions each morning: landslides above Besisahar can close the valley road for a day or more.

experiences.title: Morning hike to Lamjung Durbar above town
experiences.summary: Above Besisahar lies Gausahar, the hilltop seat of the old Lamjung kingdom, where a rebuilt palace and temples look out over the Marsyangdi valley. A short morning hike for trekkers with a spare half day before the jeep ride north.
body: Before the unification of Nepal in the 18th century, Lamjung was one of a group of small hill kingdoms, and its rulers were closely linked to the Shah dynasty of neighbouring Gorkha that went on to unify the country. The old fortified palace, known as Lamjung Durbar, stood on the ridge at Gausahar above modern Besisahar. What stands today is largely rebuilt, but the site, temples and views explain why the kings chose this ridge.

From the town centre, a path and stretches of road climb steadily through farmland and small settlements to the ridge, a gain of several hundred metres in about 1.5–2 hours. Early morning is best, when the air is cool and the northern peaks, including Lamjung Himal, sometimes show above the valley haze. Local families come up for festivals and picnics, but on most days the site is quiet. Sunday mornings are quietest, before families arrive with picnic lunches.

The hike suits trekkers who arrive in Besisahar early or have a weather delay. It is also a gentle leg-stretcher after a long bus ride from Kathmandu. Ask your guide or hotel for the current path, since new roads have cut across parts of the old trail. Carry water and sun protection, as most of the route is exposed once you leave the town. Allow time to be back at the jeep stand by early afternoon if you are booked on the next morning's departure north.

faqs.q: How long is the hike to Lamjung Durbar from Besisahar?
faqs.a: Allow about 1.5–2 hours up and 1–1.5 hours down, so 3–4 hours return with time at the top. The route is a mix of footpath and dirt road climbing steadily through farmland. Exact directions change as new roads are built, so ask your guide or hotel staff for the current path before you set off.

If you have a spare morning in Besisahar, yes. It gives context on Nepal's history of small hill kingdoms before unification and offers wide views of the Marsyangdi valley. It is not a grand monument: much is rebuilt and simple. Do not delay your circuit schedule for it, but it is a good use of a free half day.

faqs.q: Can I see the mountains from Besisahar?
faqs.a: From the town itself, views are limited by the surrounding ridges and frequent haze. From higher ground such as Gausahar, clear mornings in October to February can show Lamjung Himal and other snow peaks to the north. For close mountain views you need to head up the Marsyangdi valley towards Chame and Pisang.

experiences.title: Ghale Gaun homestay add-on from Besisahar
experiences.price_hint: ≈ ₹3,000–4,500 per person per night with meals
experiences.summary: Ghale Gaun is a Gurung hill village above the Marsyangdi valley, about 2–3 hours by jeep from Besisahar, known for its community homestay programme, cultural dances and views towards Lamjung Himal and the Annapurnas. A good add-on before or after the circuit.
body: Ghale Gaun sits on a hilltop at around 2,000 m east of the Marsyangdi, reached by a rough road from Besisahar or Khudi in roughly 2–3 hours. It was one of the first villages in this part of Nepal to organise community homestays, where guests stay in family houses, eat with their hosts and join an evening programme of Gurung songs and dances performed by the village mothers' group. Rooms are bookable through the community committee.

Mornings start with tea on the terrace and, when the weather is clear, a long line of snow peaks to the north: Lamjung Himal, Annapurna II and the Manaslu range in the distance. Walks around the village visit the small museum, the old stone houses, terraced fields and viewpoints. Many men from Ghale Gaun served in the Gurkha regiments, and the village carries that history with pride. On clear days the light on the peaks is best in the first hour after dawn.

Homestays are basic but warm: shared bathrooms, simple rooms and generous meals of dal bhat, local vegetables and sometimes millet bread or home-made snacks. Payment goes to the host family and the community fund. We add one or two nights here for travellers who want a cultural pause before the long walk to Manang, or a soft landing after the circuit if they exit back down the valley. Bring small notes in rupees, as change is scarce in the village.

faqs.q: How far is Ghale Gaun from Besisahar?
faqs.a: Ghale Gaun is about 2–3 hours by jeep from Besisahar on a rough hill road, depending on conditions. Walkers can also hike up from the Marsyangdi valley in about 5–6 hours. The road can be slow or closed after heavy rain, so in the monsoon allow extra time and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is a homestay in Ghale Gaun like?
faqs.a: You stay with a Gurung family in their house, usually in a simple private room with shared toilet facilities. Meals are home-cooked dal bhat, vegetables and local snacks, eaten with the family. In the evening there is often a cultural programme organised by the community. It is comfortable but basic; bring a torch and warm layers for the evening.

faqs.q: Can Ghale Gaun be combined with the Annapurna Circuit?
faqs.a: Yes. The simplest way is to add one or two nights before the circuit: drive from Kathmandu to Besisahar, continue to Ghale Gaun, then return to Besisahar for the jeep north. It adds 2–3 days to the overall trip. It also works at the end if you return down the Marsyangdi rather than exiting via Jomsom.

experiences.title: Walk the lower Marsyangdi to Bhulbhule
experiences.summary: For trekkers who want to start the circuit on foot rather than in a jeep, the first stage from Besisahar to Bhulbhule follows the Marsyangdi past rice terraces, suspension bridges and small Gurung and Brahmin hamlets, rising only about 80 m.
body: Walking out of Besisahar is how the Annapurna Circuit began for decades, and it is still possible. The first stage north to Bhulbhule at 840 m covers roughly 8–10 km and gains only about 80 m, following the Marsyangdi through farmland. Where the main road hugs one bank, sections of the New Annapurna Trekking Trail cross to the other on suspension bridges, giving quieter walking through villages and fields. Your guide knows which bridges are currently open.

In October and November the terraces are gold with ripening rice, and threshing is done by hand on flat stone yards beside the houses. The air is warm, 25 °C or more at midday, so walkers start early. Waterfalls drop from the side valleys, and the first glimpse of snow peaks, usually Ngadi Chuli or Himalchuli to the east, appears on clear mornings before the haze builds. Carry at least 1.5 litres of water, since tea shops are spaced out on this stretch.

Bhulbhule has a few simple lodges and a waterfall beside the bridge. From there, walkers continue over the following days via Bahundanda, Jagat and Tal towards Chame, a total of about 5 days on foot. Many people now drive this section and save their legs for the high country, but for slow travellers this lower valley is a gentle and authentic start. Rooms in Bhulbhule cost little, and the riverside setting makes a calm first night on the trail before the climb to Bahundanda.

faqs.q: Is it worth walking from Besisahar instead of driving?
faqs.a: It depends on your time and interests. Walking the lower valley adds 3–4 days through subtropical farmland, rice terraces and waterfalls, with gradual acclimatisation. The downside is sections shared with the dusty road. If you have three weeks, walk it using the side trails; if you have two weeks, drive to Chame and spend the time higher up.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk from Besisahar to Bhulbhule?
faqs.a: About 3–4 hours for most walkers, covering roughly 8–10 km with very little height gain, from 760 m to 840 m. The trail mixes road, farm tracks and footpaths on the opposite bank. Start before 9 am in autumn to avoid the midday heat, which can reach the high 20s Celsius in the valley floor.

faqs.q: Are there leeches on the lower Marsyangdi?
faqs.a: In the monsoon, from June to September, yes: the damp forests and fields of the lower valley have leeches, and the paths are muddy. From October to May they are rarely a problem. If you walk in the wet months, wear long trousers tucked into socks and carry salt or insect repellent to remove any that attach.

faqs.q: How do I get from Kathmandu to Besisahar?
faqs.a: By road. Local and tourist buses and private cars cover the roughly 175 km in 6–7 hours, via the Prithvi Highway to Dumre and then north up the Marsyangdi. Buses leave from Kathmandu early in the morning. A private car costs more but saves time and lets you stop when you wish. There are no flights to Besisahar.

faqs.q: How far is Besisahar from Pokhara?
faqs.a: About 110 km, or roughly 4 hours by road. You drive east on the Prithvi Highway to Dumre and turn north into the Marsyangdi valley. Local buses run several times a day, and private jeeps and cars are available. Many trekkers who finish the circuit in Pokhara begin by taking this road to Besisahar.

faqs.q: Can I drive from Besisahar to Manang?
faqs.a: Yes. Jeeps now run all the way from Besisahar to Manang in about 9–10 hours, though the road is rough and frequently blocked by landslides in the monsoon. Driving straight to 3,519 m carries an altitude sickness risk, so plan at least two nights in Manang before going higher. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need an ACAP permit at Besisahar?
faqs.a: Yes. Besisahar is where the Annapurna Conservation Area permit is first checked on the circuit, and you cannot buy it on the spot in most cases. Get it in Kathmandu or Pokhara beforehand. It costs NPR 3,000 for foreigners and NPR 1,000 for SAARC nationals, including Indians. Check current status before you travel.

Yes, several banks with ATMs line the main road, and it is the last place on the circuit where cash withdrawal is reliable. Chame and Manang have had ATMs in some seasons, but they often run out of cash or go offline. Withdraw enough for at least a week of teahouse spending in Besisahar, Kathmandu or Pokhara.

faqs.q: Is Besisahar worth an overnight stay?
faqs.a: It is a practical rather than scenic stop. If you leave Kathmandu early you can sometimes reach Besisahar and continue by jeep the same day, but the drive is long. An overnight makes the next morning's jeep ride to Chame easier and gives you time to buy supplies, collect cash and check gear.

faqs.q: How much is a jeep from Besisahar to Chame?
faqs.a: Shared jeep seats to Chame have recently cost roughly NPR 2,500–3,500 per person, and a private jeep roughly NPR 20,000–28,000 for the vehicle. Prices are set by local transport committees and rise with fuel costs, so check current status before you travel. Our circuit packages include private transport from Besisahar to Chame.

faqs.q: What is the weather like in Besisahar?
faqs.a: Besisahar is at 760 m, so it is warm for most of the year. October and November bring days of 24–28 °C and cool nights. December and January are mild, with days around 18–20 °C. April and May are hot, often above 30 °C. June to September is the monsoon, with heavy rain and frequent road disruptions.

faqs.q: Where does the Annapurna Circuit start?
faqs.a: Traditionally in Besisahar, the district headquarters of Lamjung. Today many trekkers drive further, to Bhulbhule, Jagat, Dharapani or Chame, and start walking there to avoid the road. The circuit then runs anticlockwise via Manang, over Thorong La at 5,416 m to Muktinath and down to Jomsom, where most people fly or drive to Pokhara.
